steps.title: The very, very, very long speech
paragraphs: Jaden’s class captain speech began: “I will be a very good captain. I play very good, I am very, very organised, and I think it would be very fun.”
His teacher counted six “very”s in four sentences, and one “play good” that should have been “play well”.
His second draft: “I will be a dependable captain. I play well, I plan every practice, and I would love the job.” Shorter, stronger, and every word earns its place.

cards.title: Good or well?
cards.body: Good is an adjective: it describes a noun (a good game) or comes after a linking verb (the soup smells good, I feel good). Well is an adverb: it tells how an action is done (she sings well, we played well). Test it: is the word telling how someone did something? Use well.

cards.title: The same trap
cards.body: After an action verb, use the adverb: ran quickly (not quick), played badly (not bad), answered correctly (not correct). “Real” describes nouns (a real diamond); to make a word stronger, use “really”. After a linking verb, keep the adjective: I feel bad, the room went quiet.

cards.title: Ditch “very”
cards.telling: very big · very tired · very cold · very angry · very funny · ran very quickly
cards.showing: enormous · exhausted · freezing · furious · hilarious · sprinted
cards.note: “Very” props up a weak word. One precise word is shorter and stronger, especially in essays.

cards.title: When “very” is fine
cards.text: the very first time · thank you very much · very well, let’s begin
cards.note: “Very” is fine in fixed phrases like these. The goal is not to ban the word, but to notice when it is propping up something weak.

prompts: Explain the difference between good and well in your own words, with an example of each.
Which “very” do you use most often? What strong word will you use instead?
